# KODE: Mining Implicit Domain Knowledge from Historical Experience for Text-to-SQL

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#kode)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-emnlp.2032.pdf) · Findings of EMNLP 2026 proceedings, pp. 43245–43266

**Reading coverage:** All 22 pages: main sections 1–4 and limitations; Appendices A–D, operator contracts, all five prompt templates, split/implementation descriptions, ablations, sensitivity, convergence and efficiency tables.

## Research question

User questions omit domain conventions such as bridge joins, derived metrics and default filters, while historical question–SQL pairs may already encode them.

## Method

KODE aligns language-evidence and SQL graphs, extracts unmatched regions into five reusable template families, and retrieves rules before exemplars. A critic localizes conflicts for bounded rewriting. Optional backfill promotes queries with execution consensus and no detected residual conflict, with versioning and conflict rollback.

## Evaluation

Controlled ScienceBenchmark comparisons test in-domain reuse; BIRD/Spider schema-disjoint experiments transfer delexicalized templates. A separate BIRD-Dev-Domain split uses 460 history examples and 1,074 test queries with human evidence withheld. Ablations isolate knowledge types; five sequential batches assess deployment accumulation with frozen within-batch memory.

## What the results support

Reported ScienceBenchmark average execution accuracy improves by 11.1 points over the strongest controlled comparator; abstract transfer gains are smaller, 2.0–3.2 points. Automatic backfill reaches 92.1% execution-based promotion precision at 47.6% coverage and improves later batches relative to frozen empty memory.

## Limits and qualifications

Historical conventions can encode systematic mistakes or preferences that do not match a new user. Graph well-formedness and execution consensus cannot establish semantic correctness. The sequential experiment uses one fixed shuffled order and measures promotion by execution, not human intent. Latency excludes mining and ongoing audits; schema drift, adversarial logs and long-lived memory were not evaluated.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

A concrete alternative to user clarification when trusted domain history supplies missing context, while exposing the unresolved need to decide when historical defaults are insufficient or unsafe to reuse.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Critic acceptance certifies semantic correctness. | The operator-contract appendix explicitly limits checks to graph well-formedness; promotion relies on six of eight execution-equivalent candidates and no detected conflicts. | §2.3, equations 8–9; Appendix D.1 | Treat as heuristic filtering, not semantic proof or calibrated correctness. |
| All domain knowledge transfers across schemas. | The transfer protocol excludes source-specific concepts, values and concrete joins and transfers only typed/delexicalized structures. | §3.4 and Table 5 | Restrict transfer claims to abstract templates. |
| Deployment accumulation eliminates erroneous memory. | The paper reports 92.1% promotion precision, acknowledges contamination and uses only one fixed shuffled prequential order. | §3.1 Statistical Reporting; §3.6/Table 9; Limitations | Qualify as controlled evidence of filtered accumulation with residual errors. |
